title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition is dominated by Election Day in the US midterms. It covers the Supreme Court's refusal to let the administration set aside 20,000 California ballots, and the fallout from Rep. Haley Stevens endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan. Elsewhere: Apple's first earnings under its new CEO, the postponement of football's Asian Cup, a helicopter collision near Everest, a sharp drop in Korean stocks, and local Charlotte news.

stories.headline: Apple reports record September quarter as foldable iPhone Duo stays in short supply
stories.summary: Apple reported its first quarterly results under new CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook in September. Revenue rose 12% to about $114.5bn, and iPhone revenue grew 17% to about $57.6bn. The company said its new foldable iPhone Duo, priced near $2,000, is supply-constrained, and it could not predict when supply will meet demand. Ternus described memory-chip price increases tied to the AI data-centre boom as 'unprecedented', and Apple has raised prices across its products. In South Korea, sales of Samsung's rival Galaxy Z Fold8 rose about 20% in the week after the Duo launched, though a causal link has not been shown.
key_facts: Quarterly revenue was $114.5bn, up 12%. iPhone revenue was about $57.6bn, up 17%.
Mac revenue was about $10.8bn. Outlets reported growth of 24% (The Verge, Fox Business) or 27% (BBC).
iPad revenue fell 10%. The Duo's sales are not included in this quarter.
Apple acknowledged on Oct. 26 that a 'small number' of Duo screens cracked along the fold and offered replacements.
Galaxy Z Fold8 sales in Korea rose more than 20% in the week of Oct. 23-29 compared with the prior week, according to telecom industry figures.

perspectives.framing: The Verge focused on the iPhone revenue record despite there being no new standard model. It linked the growth to pricier Pro models and price increases, and noted other product launches such as a touchscreen MacBook Pro.

The BBC highlighted the Duo shortage and its screen problems, noting executives did not mention the defects on the earnings call, and set this against memory-cost pressures and price rises. Korean outlets focused on Samsung's sales gain. The Korea Herald stressed that there is no evidence linking the gain to Apple's problems, while Yonhap cited industry sources crediting Samsung's durability and AI features.

Fox Business framed the results as a record quarter and best-ever fiscal year under the new CEO, beating Wall Street estimates. It quoted Ternus at length on supply, memory costs and the Mac's 'AI moment', and noted analyst doubts about whether the iPhone 18 can match the iPhone 17's upgrade cycle.

disputed: The cause of the Duo screen cracking has not been established, and the scale of returns is unclear. Ternus said 'a very small percentage' of units were returned.
Whether Samsung's Korean sales gain reflects buyers switching from Apple is unconfirmed.
Outlets reported different Mac growth figures: 24% versus 27%.
stories.why: The results show how AI-driven chip and memory costs are pushing up prices for consumer electronics.

stories.headline: Democrat Haley Stevens defends endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
stories.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers two days before the election. The endorsement followed a dispute over an outside group's ad that blamed the cost of living on US support for Israel; El-Sayed's campaign then disinvited her. Democratic leaders including Chuck Schumer and Nancy Pelosi condemned the move, Michigan's Democratic Party chair said she is not a party member, and several of her staff resigned. Stevens called it 'a decision of conscience' and said suggestions that her fiancé influenced her were sexist. Vice President JD Vance said the endorsement 'certainly' helps Rogers.
key_facts: Stevens announced her endorsement of Rogers on Sunday, two days before Election Day.
El-Sayed's campaign said it raised more than $2.4m after the endorsement, including from more than 26,000 first-time donors.
Schumer called the endorsement 'a despicable betrayal'.
Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, backed Rogers the week before, citing El-Sayed's stance on Israel.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian emphasised Democratic outrage, quoting Schumer, Pelosi, Zohran Mamdani and the state party chair, and described Stevens as evasive in a CNN interview. PBS interviewed Rep. Debbie Dingell, who called the endorsement a 'huge distraction', condemned hateful ads on all sides, and described fears in the Arab American community.
The Hill focused on Stevens' own explanation, including her conclusion that El-Sayed is 'not fit to serve' and her concerns about campaign ads.

Fox News led with Vance's comments calling El-Sayed 'a crazy person'. It highlighted El-Sayed's ties to streamer Hasan Piker and Rogers' accusations about 'terrorist sympathizers'. The New York Post and Washington Examiner centred on Stevens' 'sexism' rebuttal and her criticism of the Democratic backlash as intolerance of dissent.

disputed: What triggered the endorsement. Stevens cites conscience and the ad dispute, while critics point to sour grapes after the primary or her fiancé's influence.
Dingell said Stevens had told her she would not endorse Rogers.
The effect on the race's outcome is unknown.
stories.why: Michigan is seen as pivotal to control of the Senate, and the episode exposes Democratic divisions over Israel.

stories.headline: Americans vote in midterms that will decide control of Congress
stories.summary: Voters are choosing all 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats and 36 state governors. The cost of living is the top concern, with the war with Iran and tariffs cited as factors behind higher prices. Democrats are widely expected to retake the House, while the Senate is seen as close. Final polls cited by The Guardian show Democrats ahead in several races in traditionally Republican states. President Trump, facing low approval ratings, said a sitting president usually 'doesn't win the midterms' and called Democratic candidates 'dangerous'; House Democrats announced election-observation efforts amid his unsubstantiated fraud claims.
key_facts: Republicans hold a 218-214 House majority and 53 Senate seats. Democrats need a net gain of four in each chamber.
The president's party has lost House seats in 18 of the past 20 midterms.
Diesel rose from $3.75 before the war began in February to a record $6.52 in September, according to the BBC.
House Democrats plan to deploy about 300 staff as observers in 60-70 close races.
Final NYT/Siena polls put Democrats ahead in five of seven key battleground contests, according to The Guardian.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and Al Jazeera framed the vote as a referendum on Trump's agenda, highlighting Iran, the economy and AI as issues. NPR offered a guide to House races, describing Republicans as facing severe headwinds.

The BBC emphasised Republican vulnerability in safe states and asked whether Trump is still an electoral asset. Deutsche Welle paired Trump's closing remarks with Schumer's response and a reported US strike on Iran. WBTV focused on Democrats' election-security plans and noted that fraud prosecutions have been few.

disputed: Trump's voter-fraud claims are described by outlets as unsubstantiated.
A US strike on Iran's Qeshm Island was reported by the Wall Street Journal but not confirmed by US Central Command.
stories.why: The outcome sets the balance of power for the final two years of Trump's term.

stories.headline: 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia moved to December 2027 after Houthi attacks
stories.summary: The Asian Football Confederation rescheduled the 24-team tournament. It was due to run from Jan. 7 to Feb. 5, 2027, and will now run from Dec. 23, 2027, to Jan. 21, 2028. The AFC cited 'exceptional circumstances' including logistical complexities and travel disruptions. Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi missile attacks, including a strike on Riyadh's airport in October. The new dates need FIFA approval.
key_facts: The new dates are Dec. 23, 2027, to Jan. 21, 2028.
The October attack on Riyadh airport killed 13 people (BBC) or at least 12 (CNA), and wounded more than 300.
Other Saudi events, including golf's Asian Tour season-ending event, have been postponed or cancelled.
This is the second successive Asian Cup to be postponed.

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera stressed the ongoing Houthi-Saudi hostilities and security concerns raised by participating nations.

The BBC focused on the effect on Premier League clubs and Japanese players. CNA noted Saudi Arabia's sports investments, its 2034 World Cup hosting plans, and Singapore's qualification. Yonhap and the Korea Herald highlighted uncertainty over South Korea's caretaker coach and the Korea Football Association's leadership election.

disputed: The airport attack death toll differs: 13 in the BBC versus at least 12 in CNA.
FIFA approval of the new dates is pending.
stories.why: The decision shows how regional conflict is disrupting Saudi Arabia's push to host major sporting events.

stories.headline: Supreme Court declines Justice Department bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
stories.summary: On Monday, hours after the request, the Supreme Court denied a Justice Department application to block California from counting mail ballots from about 20,000 voters the administration says are likely noncitizens. The one-sentence order gave no reasoning and noted no dissents. Lower courts had already rejected the request, and state officials and analysts said the list contained many errors. A separate federal judge barred the Justice Department from threatening election workers.
key_facts: The order was unsigned, with no noted dissents, and California was not asked to respond first.
More than six million mail ballots had been received in California as of Sunday night.
A Justice Department lawyer acknowledged the noncitizen lists had a 'high error rate', according to MS NOW as cited by CNBC.
Judge David Carter wrote that never before had the federal government sought to coerce a state on the eve of an election.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian called the ruling the latest 'judicial rebuke' of unprecedented federal intervention, and tied it to Trump's low approval ratings and other campaign news.

Outlets broadly framed the ruling as a legal blow to the administration. CNBC quoted California AG Rob Bonta calling the bid a 'Hail Mary' and also laid out the Solicitor General's argument. The BBC and Deutsche Welle stressed errors in the list and research showing voter fraud is rare. Axios noted the administration says it is defending election law.

disputed: Whether any of the flagged voters are actually noncitizens. A filed analysis found thousands of apparent US citizens on the list.
The Justice Department's separate appeal in Alaska is ongoing.
stories.why: The ruling sets limits on federal intervention in how states run and count elections.

stories.headline: Helicopter collision in Everest region kills Indian tourist
stories.summary: Two helicopters, operated by Fishtail Air and Dynasty Air, collided while landing in Nepal's Everest region on Tuesday. An Indian tourist was killed and a New Zealander was injured; the Associated Press-style report in the New York Post said a Nepali pilot was also hurt. Fishtail said its aircraft was carrying rescued passengers, while Dynasty said its helicopter carried only cargo. The crash came during peak trekking season.
key_facts: The 47-year-old Indian tourist died, according to the NY Post.
The New Zealand passenger was taken to Kathmandu for treatment.
The collision was reported at Pheriche, at 13,780 feet, according to the NY Post.

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera gave a brief factual account.
CNA cited local officials and statements from both operators.
The New York Post added details on the location, the injured pilot, and helicopters' role in evacuating trekkers.

disputed: The location is described differently: base camp area (CNA) versus Pheriche below base camp (NY Post).
The total number of people aboard is unclear.
stories.why: Helicopters are a lifeline for trekkers in the Everest region during its busiest season.

stories.headline: Carolinas Election Day guide; UNC wins Malone's coaching debut
stories.summary: WFAE outlined voting rules for the Carolinas: North Carolina polls are open 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., photo ID is required in both states, and voters must use their assigned precinct. Queen City News noted that Senate races in both Carolinas and a western North Carolina House seat could affect control of Congress. Separately, North Carolina beat Western Carolina 80-72 in former Nuggets coach Michael Malone's debut.
key_facts: South Carolina polls are open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Matt Able scored 18 points for UNC.
Malone won the 2023 NBA title with Denver.

perspectives.framing: WFAE offered practical voter information.
Queen City News stressed the national stakes of the local races, and WBTV ran Associated Press game coverage.

stories.why: Local voters need to know the rules, and Carolina races could help decide Senate control.

stories.headline: Charlotte to extend exclusive talks with Gateway Station developer
stories.summary: Charlotte plans to keep negotiating with Charlotte Gateway Partners through the end of the year on Gateway Station. The planned mixed-use project at an uptown Amtrak station site has been delayed for more than a decade. The new Metropolitan Public Transportation Authority is expected to join as a partner in 2027.
key_facts: Phase one, which added track improvements and the Amtrak platform, finished in 2022.
Deputy City Manager Allyson Craig called it 'the most transit-connected project' in the city.

perspectives.framing: WFAE detailed the city's plans and the uncertainty over who will lead the project.
WCNC emphasised that the timeline remains at a standstill.

disputed: Whether the city will hand the project to the Metropolitan Public Transportation Authority is unclear.
stories.why: The project is central to Charlotte's transit-oriented growth plans.

stories.headline: National Guard roles at midterms; Memphis shooting video released
stories.summary: The Hill reported that National Guard members in at least seven states will support the elections, including ballot-box monitoring in Washington state and cybersecurity work in Iowa and Colorado. Separately, Shelby County prosecutors released video of a July shooting in Memphis in which a Tennessee Guard member serving on a federal task force fatally shot Tyrin Johnson, 20. An autopsy shared by Johnson's family found he was shot in the back, contradicting the official account that he pointed a gun at the guard members. No charging decision has been made.
key_facts: Guard members in at least seven states have election roles.
Johnson, who was armed, died from a single gunshot on July 5.
The task force was involved in four fatal shootings between May and July.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian focused on the Memphis footage showing troops pointing guns at the dying man, and on the conflict between the autopsy and official accounts.
The Hill gave a factual rundown of Guard election deployments.

disputed: Whether Johnson pointed a gun at the guard members. The released footage does not show the shooting itself.
The investigation by the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation is ongoing.
stories.why: Military involvement around elections and policing remains contentious.

stories.headline: KOSPI falls 3.59% amid AI spending concerns
stories.summary: South Korea's benchmark KOSPI index closed down 3.59% at 5,648.79, led by chip stocks, after US tech shares fell. Analysts cited doubts over returns on heavy AI infrastructure spending and caution ahead of the US midterms. Oil refiners also dropped as crude prices fell on hopes of US-Iran diplomacy.
key_facts: Samsung Electronics fell 4.15% and SK hynix fell 5.03%.
S-Oil dropped 11.77%.
Foreign investors were net sellers of 1.5 trillion won.

perspectives.framing: Yonhap and the Korea Herald gave straightforward market reports focused on AI profitability worries.

stories.why: The sell-off signals growing investor doubt about the AI investment boom.
